header.workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols

sourceStatement: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), {cite}, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.
aboutDefault: Read the Secret History knowing what it is: the Mongolian original, in Mongolian script, is lost. What survives is a Ming-dynasty teaching edition made at the Hanlin Academy, in which the Mongolian was written out phonetically in Chinese characters, with a Chinese gloss over every word, so that interpreters could learn the language. So the characters on this page are Chinese, and mean nothing in Chinese; they are the sounds of the Mongol words. The Mongol word is the line beneath, and it is a reconstruction — scholars differ over the vowels, and the Chinese script cannot show some distinctions at all. The glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators' own, six hundred years old. Tap a word for both. A few of the characters are rare enough that some devices have no font for them and will show an empty box.
